unit.title: Teaching embedded and IoT systems at university

lesson.title: IoT protocols: MQTT, CoAP and LoRa
lesson.subtitle: Choosing how devices talk

video.title: IoT protocols: MQTT, CoAP and LoRa: Choosing how devices talk
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A cooperative asked us to monitor soil moisture across forty hectares. There is no Wi-Fi, no mains power, and the nearest mobile mast is eight kilometres away. Which network would you choose?

scenes.on_screen_text: IoT protocols: MQTT, CoAP and LoRa
scenes.narration: Today: how publish and subscribe works, when to use MQTT or CoAP, and the trade-off between range, data rate and energy in LoRa and mesh networks.
In MQTT, devices never talk to each other directly. A sensor publishes to a topic on a broker. Any client that subscribed to that topic receives the message. Senders and receivers stay decoupled.
MQTT offers three delivery levels. Zero means at most once, with no acknowledgement. One means at least once, so duplicates are possible. Two means exactly once, at the cost of a four-step handshake.
Typical ranges in open country: Bluetooth Low Energy tens of metres, Wi-Fi around a hundred, Zigbee mesh a few hundred per hop, and LoRa several kilometres, but at only a few kilobits per second.
CoAP, defined in RFC seven two five two, brings a web-like request and response model to tiny devices over UDP. It suits small nodes that are asked for readings, while MQTT suits streams of events.

scenes.on_screen_text: Teach it with a design brief
scenes.narration: Protocol lectures become lists of acronyms. Instead, give teams a real brief with distance, power and data needs. Make them choose and justify a stack, then test it on hardware.
Quick check! A sensor sends a temperature every ten seconds, and an occasional lost reading does not matter. Which MQTT quality of service fits best?
Level zero. The next reading arrives in ten seconds, so acknowledgements would only cost energy. Save higher levels for commands, such as opening a valve.
In the app, open the mesh lab. Break a sensor and watch the messages find a new route to the gateway, then add relays where the range runs out.
Your turn. Forty hectares, no power, readings every fifteen minutes, a few bytes each. Which link fits best?
LoRa, with one gateway. Remember: publish and subscribe decouples devices, choose the lowest quality of service that is safe, and trade data rate for range.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lab
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lab: set up a free MQTT broker on a laptop. Each team publishes sensor readings to its own topic, and subscribes to another team's.

checkpoints.prompt: Temperature every 10 s; an occasional loss doesn't matter. Which MQTT QoS?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: acknowledgements would only cost energy when the next reading comes soon.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: higher QoS adds messages and energy; for frequent, replaceable readings, QoS 0 is enough.

checkpoints.prompt: 40 hectares, no power, a few bytes every 15 minutes. Which link?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: LoRa reaches kilometres on little energy, and the data need is tiny.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: Wi-Fi and BLE reach tens to hundreds of metres; LoRa covers kilometres at low rates.
